flavorsExplorer.aboutP1: The Coffee Flavor Wheel is a structured vocabulary that the specialty coffee community uses to talk about taste. It is read from the inside out: the inner ring shows broad categories (Fruity, Floral, Nutty/Cocoa, Sweet, and so on), the middle ring breaks each category into subcategories (Berry, Citrus, Brown Sugar…), and the outer ring lists specific notes a taster might actually call out — blackberry, bergamot, caramel.
flavorsExplorer.aboutP2: The original wheel was developed by the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) and World Coffee Research as a research-backed consensus on how baristas, roasters, and Q-graders describe the sensory experience of brewed coffee. Coffees are tasted against this lexicon during cupping so that profiles can be compared consistently across origins and roasts.
flavorsExplorer.aboutP3: On this page, click anywhere on the wheel to filter the bean catalog. Tap an outer note to find a single flavor, tap a subcategory to broaden the search, or tap a category to see every bean whose profile touches that family.

about.heading: About BeanMap
about.lead: BeanMap is a free, open-source atlas of specialty coffee. It answers three questions about any bean — where on Earth it grew, what it tastes like, and how to brew it — starting from a spinnable globe rather than a list.

about.dataBody1: Every origin profile is written by hand from published producer and importer information, cupping notes, and regional harvest data, then tagged against the SCA flavor lexicon. Coordinates mark the growing region, not a single farm — most of these origins are hundreds of smallholders rather than one estate.
about.dataBody2: Flavor profiles are scored on six axes — acidity, body, sweetness, bitterness, complexity, and fruitiness — from 1 to 10. That is a deliberate simplification: it exists so origins can be compared at a glance, not to replace cupping. Two coffees with the same radar shape can still taste quite different in the cup.
about.dataBody3: Brewing recipes are starting points — grind size, water temperature, ratio, and a pour schedule — with an affinity score for how well each method suits that bean. Your grinder, your water, and the roast date all move the target, which is exactly why there is a brewing journal for recording what actually worked.
about.openHeading: Open source, no ads, nothing for sale
about.openBody: BeanMap sells no coffee, runs no ads, and takes no affiliate commission. It is an independent side project, not a roaster or a retailer, and it is not affiliated with any of the farms, cooperatives, or brands it describes. Code and catalog are both MIT-licensed on GitHub, so corrections and new origins are very welcome as pull requests.
about.privacyBody: Everything here works signed out: the map, search, filters, comparison, brewing calculator, timer, and all the Learn articles are public and static. Signing in with Google or GitHub adds exactly two things — favorites that follow you between devices, and a private brewing journal only you can read.

what.a: BeanMap is a free, interactive world map of specialty coffee. It plots {beans} coffee origins from {countries} countries onto a 3D globe; clicking a marker opens that origin's flavor profile, altitude, processing method, harvest season, and recommended brewing recipes.

free.a: Yes. BeanMap is free and open source under the MIT license. There is no paywall, no advertising, no affiliate link, and no account required.

data.q: Where does BeanMap's coffee data come from?
data.a: Origin profiles are compiled by hand from published producer and importer information, cupping notes, and regional harvest data, then tagged against the SCA flavor lexicon ({categories} categories, {subcategories} subcategories, {notes} notes). Coordinates mark the growing region rather than an individual farm.

buy.q: Can I buy coffee on BeanMap?
buy.a: No. BeanMap is a reference atlas, not a shop. It has no storefront and no commercial relationship with any roaster — use it to work out what you want, then buy it wherever you like.

pick.q: How do I find a coffee I will enjoy?
pick.a: Start from a flavor you already like. Open the flavor wheel and click a note such as blackcurrant or jasmine, and the map filters down to origins that taste that way. You can also filter by altitude, processing method, and roast level, or compare up to three beans side by side.

beanBelt.a: The Bean Belt is the band around the equator, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn at roughly 23.44° north and south, where virtually all commercial coffee grows. BeanMap draws it directly on the globe so the pattern is visible at a glance.

account.a: No. The map, search, filters, comparison, brewing calculator, timer, and all {articles} Learn articles work signed out. An account only adds favorites that sync between devices and a private brewing journal.

origins.q: Which countries grow the coffee on BeanMap?
origins.a: {countries} of them. East African origins — Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda — lean floral with bright acidity; Latin American ones such as Colombia, Guatemala, Costa Rica, and Brazil sit in balanced caramel-and-cocoa territory; Asian origins like Indonesia, Vietnam, and India tend to be heavy-bodied and low in acid. The home page lists every producing country, and each one opens that country's beans on the map.

flavorWheel.q: How do I read the coffee flavor wheel?
flavorWheel.a: The SCA wheel runs from {categories} broad families at the center — fruity, floral, nutty/cocoa — outward to {notes} specific tasting notes. Read it inside-out: name the family first, then move outward for the closest description. Click any segment on BeanMap and the map filters to the origins that taste like it.

home.heading: Explore coffee origins on an interactive world map
home.lead: BeanMap plots {beans} specialty coffee origins from {countries} countries onto a spinnable globe. Click a marker to fly to the growing region, read its flavor profile as a six-axis radar, and get a brewing recipe tuned to that particular bean — grind, water temperature, ratio, and pour schedule.
home.beanBeltHeading: Why everything sits near the equator
home.beanBeltBody: Arabica needs a narrow band of altitude, rainfall, and temperature that only really exists between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn — roughly 23.44° north and south. BeanMap draws that band, the Bean Belt, straight onto the globe, which is why Ethiopia, Colombia, and Indonesia keep turning up on your bag of beans.
